source: MacGregor & Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: Decomposition means breaking a hard-to-estimate quantity into multiplicative parts, estimating each, and recombining. Raiffa (1968) called it the spirit of decision analysis. Three conditions for it to work: the target is hard to estimate, part errors are relatively smaller than target error, and part errors are not strongly positively correlated.
numbers: Error compounding example: two part errors of +20 percent in the same direction give +44 percent in the target (1.2 x 1.2 = 1.44).
limits: The conditions are hard to state in operational terms. Additive splits are called disaggregation and are out of scope.
agent_relevance: Checklist for O3: decompose only if the whole is hard, the parts are easier, and part errors are roughly independent.

source: Armstrong, Denniston & Gordon (1975) The use of the decomposition principle in making judgments (read only through the description in MacGregor & Armstrong 1994; original blocked)
finding: Founding study. 151 subjects were randomly split into decomposed and direct groups. Problems were quantities such as packs of Polaroid film used in the US in 1970. Decomposition improved accuracy, most when the subject knew little. Authors concluded it usually helps and is unlikely to hurt.
numbers: N=151. MA94 reanalysis: on 3 extreme, high-uncertainty problems median error ratio fell from 18.0 (global) to 5.7 (decomposed), a gain of 12.3. One non-extreme problem gained less.
limits: Not read first-hand. The claim 'unlikely to hurt' was later shown wrong for easy problems. The 1975 paper had a typo (66.5 billion for 66.5 million) that was cited onward.
agent_relevance: Origin of the idea that decomposition helps most when the model knows little.

source: MacGregor, Lichtenstein & Slovic (1988) Structuring knowledge retrieval: an analysis of decomposed quantitative judgments (read only through MacGregor & Armstrong 1994; original paywalled)
finding: Second founding study. 16 almanac-style problems (physicians, marriages, imported cars, gasoline, cigarettes and so on), 45 subjects per estimate. Decomposed estimates beat global ones. Uncertainty was measured as spread across subjects (interquartile range).
numbers: MA94 reanalysis: 6 problems with extreme size (over 7 digits) and high disagreement (IQR log10 >= 1.75): global median error ratio 99.3, decomposed 3.0, reduction 96.3. 5 problems not extreme and low disagreement (IQR log10 <= 1.3): global 1.8, decomposed 2.3, so decomposition was worse (error about 50 percent higher). Correlation between digit count of true value and IQR was about +0.75.
limits: Original text not opened; numbers come from MA94. Group geometric means, not individuals.
agent_relevance: Gain is huge when the model has no feel for the magnitude and slightly negative when it does.

source: MacGregor & Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: Pooling the two earlier studies: decomposition cut error by a factor of 68.3 on nine extreme, uncertain problems and had no overall effect on the other six.
numbers: 9 extreme-uncertain problems: reduction 68.3 (weighted by number of questions). 6 other problems: about zero net effect. 'Extreme' was first more than 7 digits, then revised to 7 or more.
limits: Post hoc split made by the authors, who then ran a new experiment. The cut-off is arbitrary and unit-dependent.
agent_relevance: Decomposition is conditional, not a free default.

source: MacGregor & Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: New experiment: 280 subjects, 10 problems, 1078 estimates, random assignment to global or decomposed. Four not-extreme problems (true value 4 digits or fewer) and six extreme ones (3.5 million to 4.2 billion). Decomposition helped on extreme and hurt on not-extreme.
numbers: Extreme: better in 5 of 6; error reduction from 4.10 (athletic shoes) to 91.47 (auto accidents); area of US 33.88 -> 1.70; wheat 45.71 -> 6.92; pants 17.38 -> 10.00; TV Guide worse, 7.76 -> 10.96 (not significant). Median reduction 19.78 (about 20-fold), p<0.001 one-tail. Not extreme: median error rose 458 percent, p<0.05 two-tail; Argentine immigrants 4.89 -> 46.77; bank failures 10.45 -> 19.50; presidents 1.23 -> 1.35; coin 1.82 -> 1.41.
limits: Error ratio = max(est/true, true/est); tests on logs. Decomposition subjects got only half the problems. Two non-extreme problems had a component with the US population, which subjects misjudged by factor 1.97. Single lab, newspaper-recruited volunteers.
agent_relevance: Replication with random assignment of the extreme-value boundary. For an LLM: decompose when the target is a number it cannot anchor (very large or very small).

source: MacGregor & Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: Spread (Q3 minus Q1 in digits) shrank after decomposition on 4 of 6 extreme problems but grew on 3 of 4 non-extreme ones. Parts were easier than the whole for only 3 of 6 problems checked.
numbers: Log10 IQR global -> decomposed: area of US 2.30 -> 0.37; wheat 3.30 -> 0.89; athletic shoes 2.00 -> 1.09; Argentine immigrants 1.00 -> 2.14 (worse); TV Guide 1.36 -> 1.85 (worse).
limits: Few problems; authors say there are too few to relate IQR to error formally.
agent_relevance: Spread across samples is a cheap signal of whether decomposition is working: if sub-answers disagree more than direct ones, stop.

source: MacGregor & Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: Decomposition lowered subjects' confidence (they judged the task harder) and trimmed overconfidence a little, but both groups stayed overconfident.
numbers: Chance of being within 10 percent of the true value: global group expected 38.9 percent, got 10.9 percent (overconfidence 28.0 points). Decomposed group expected 32.6 percent, got 9.0 percent (23.6 points). Three self-rating measures of uncertainty correlated above 0.99 across 6 problems. US presidents confidence 64.4 vs 35.2.
limits: Within-10-percent is a harsh target, so hit rates are low for everyone.
agent_relevance: Decomposition improves accuracy more than calibration; a separate calibration step is still needed (links to subfield 01).

source: Ravinder, Kleinmuntz & Dyer (1988) The reliability of subjective probabilities obtained through decomposition
finding: A psychometric measurement-error model gives the random error of a decomposed estimate as a function of error size and correlation of the component assessments, compared with direct assessment as a percent change in error.
numbers: No numbers on the page (abstract only).
limits: Only the abstract page was read.
agent_relevance: Formal basis for 'parts easier, errors uncorrelated'. Parts drawn from one model share errors, so benefit may be smaller than for independent humans.

source: Henrion, Fischer & Mullin (1993) Divide and conquer? Effects of decomposition on the accuracy and calibration of subjective probability distributions
finding: Almanac quantities, five fractiles each, three conditions: direct, experimenter-set decomposition, subject-chosen decomposition. Decomposition did not significantly change median accuracy or calibration. It shifted a bias from underestimating uncertainty (direct) to overestimating it (decomposed). Experimenter and subject decompositions did not differ.
numbers: No numbers obtained. Per MA94 the US population was given to subjects and they rated components easier than the whole.
limits: Not opened: full text paywalled and the page I fetched had no abstract. Summary comes from a search-tool description of the abstract; unverified.
agent_relevance: A null result for probability distributions: decomposition helps point estimates of extreme quantities, not necessarily calibrated ranges.

source: Tetlock & Gardner (2015) Superforecasting (named as key work in SUBFIELDS.md; not read)
finding: SUBFIELDS.md lists Tetlock as the key work and notes no effect size is reported. I could not open the book. This line only records that no quantified Tetlock effect is available here.
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Do not claim a measured superforecaster gain for decomposition; the quantified evidence is the estimation studies above and the LLM work below.

source: Kalyan et al. (2021) How much coffee was consumed during EMNLP 2019? Fermi problems
finding: Two datasets: about 1,000 real Fermi problems from quizzes and olympiads and about 10,000 synthetic ones, each with a gold executable program (the decomposition) and supporting facts. Score fp_score = max(0, 1 - |log10(A/A*)|/3): full marks at the exact answer, 1/3 less per order of magnitude, zero at three or more.
numbers: Fine-tuned LMs were off by about two orders of magnitude on average (abstract).
limits: Fine-tuned T5-type models, not frontier chat models. The gold decomposition is one of many valid ones.
agent_relevance: A scoring rule and data to test whether our O3 decomposition lands in the right order of magnitude.

source: Kalyan et al. (2021) How much coffee was consumed during EMNLP 2019? Fermi problems
finding: T5 fine-tuned on synthetic, real or both. Three settings: facts supplied (task 1), facts plus distractors (task 2), question only (task 3). Executing the model's own program gave about double the direct-answer score when facts were supplied, and the question-only task was very hard.
numbers: Real FPs, perfect-context, T5 fine-tuned on real: direct answer 0.18, program-derived answer 0.36, fact F1 0.95. Fine-tuned on both: direct 0.16, program answer 0.36. Question-only task: program-derived answer scores about 0.01 to 0.04. Synthetic FPs near 1.0 with facts. Adding 10 random distractor facts did not hurt (footnote 11).
limits: Table 2 columns were partly garbled in text extraction, so single cells in task 2 and 3 should be re-checked in the PDF before citing.
agent_relevance: Explicit program-style decomposition roughly doubled accuracy when facts were known (0.36 vs 0.18); retrieving the right facts is the bottleneck.

source: Kalyan et al. (2021) How much coffee was consumed during EMNLP 2019? Fermi problems
finding: Table 3 shows failure modes: a meaningless decomposition that still lands near the answer (airborne people over Europe), a correct decomposition with a wrong fact (jelly beans in a bucket, about three orders of magnitude off) and one with missing steps (cigarettes smoked in history).
numbers: Europe airborne compiled-answer accuracy 0.98; jelly beans 0.00; cigarettes 0.00.
limits: Qualitative, three examples.
agent_relevance: A right answer can come from a bad decomposition, so score the sub-steps, not only the final number.

source: Liu et al. (2025) LLM for complex reasoning task: an exploratory study in Fermi problems
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama 3 on Kalyan's real Fermi set with a zero-shot prompt and structured prompts at TELeR levels 0, 2, 4. Every overall fp_score stayed at or below 0.500.
numbers: Overall fp_score for levels 0 / 2 / 4: GPT-3.5 0.398 / 0.420 / 0.418; GPT-4 0.466 / 0.479 / 0.500; Llama 3 0.439 / 0.469 / 0.460. 556 test questions (252 standard, 304 specific). GPT-4 level 4: standard 0.568, specific 0.499. GPT-3.5 level 0: 0.442 vs 0.367.
limits: Prompt levels vary structure, not decomposition specifically; no ablation of decompose-first. Prompts were written by an LLM. Exploratory.
agent_relevance: Prompt structure moved fp_score by only 0.03 to 0.07; vague, under-specified questions are the failure case.

source: Epstein, Winnicki, Sornwanee & Dwaraknath (2025) LLMs are overconfident: evaluating confidence interval calibration with FermiEval
finding: 1,000 Science Olympiad Fermi questions (500 train, 500 test), answers as powers of ten. GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Haiku and Grok-3-mini gave intervals at 90, 95, 99 and 99.8 percent. Coverage stayed flat as the nominal level rose.
numbers: Nominal 99 percent intervals covered the truth about 65 percent of the time on average. GPT-4o-mini baseline coverage 0.63 / 0.59 / 0.64 at nominal 0.90 / 0.95 / 0.99. Conformal adjustment gave about 99 percent coverage and cut the Winkler score by 54 percent. Log-probability method raised GPT-4o-mini coverage to 0.85 / 0.89 / 0.90.
limits: Small cheap models; tests intervals around the model's own answer, not decomposition. The perception-tunnel theory is a model, not a causal test.
agent_relevance: Fermi estimates from an LLM have intervals that are too narrow; O3 outputs need widened or conformally calibrated ranges.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: The system prompts the LM to break the forecasting question into sub-questions and uses each to write a news search query, in addition to searching the question directly. Example: for an election, sub-questions cover campaign finances, economic indicators and geopolitical events.
numbers: Pipeline: query generation, news retrieval, GPT-3.5 relevance filter (saves 70 percent cost), reasoning, trimmed-mean ensemble. The text I read reports no ablation isolating the sub-question step.
limits: Decomposition here widens search; it is not numeric recombination. No isolated effect size.
agent_relevance: Another use of O3: split the question to widen evidence gathering.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Test set of 914 questions (3,762 train, 840 validation) from forecasting platforms, after model cutoffs. Baseline LMs without retrieval were near random; the full system nears the human crowd.
numbers: Random 0.250; human crowd 0.149; best baseline GPT-4-1106-Preview zero-shot 0.208 (scratchpad 0.224). System 0.179 on all questions; accuracy 71.5 vs crowd 77.0 percent. With all selection criteria: system 0.186 vs crowd 0.162 (aggregate of system and crowd best in every setting). 14 LMs tested.
limits: Brier SE about 0.003 to 0.006. Decomposition's own share is unknown.
agent_relevance: Retrieval plus structure moved Brier from 0.224 (scratchpad) to 0.179; keep decomposition ablation as our own test.

source: Radhakrishnan et al. (2023) Question decomposition improves the faithfulness of model-generated reasoning
finding: Three methods: chain of thought, CoT decomposition (sub-questions in one context) and factored decomposition (each sub-question answered in a separate context, then recomposed). Four QA tasks. Factored decomposition gave the most faithful reasoning at some cost in accuracy.
numbers: Average accuracy: zero-shot 72.8, few-shot 79.7, chain of thought about 86.0, CoT decomposition about 85.6, factored decomposition about 81.8 (read from Figure 1 labels). Faithfulness metrics normalised 0 to 1.
limits: Table 1 cells scrambled in text extraction; the accuracy split follows Figure 1 labels. Anthropic models, QA tasks, not forecasting.
agent_relevance: Answering sub-questions in separate contexts gives checkable steps and resists bias, matching our rule that code controls steps.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in large language models
finding: Two stages: the model lists simpler sub-problems, then solves them in order, each answer feeding the next. Tested on SCAN length split, GSM8K and DROP.
numbers: SCAN length split with code-davinci-002: standard 16.7, chain of thought 16.2, least-to-most 99.7; text-davinci-002 6.0 / 0.0 / 76.0. GSM8K: CoT 60.87 vs least-to-most 62.39; by steps: 2 steps CoT 76.68 vs 74.53, 5 steps 39.07 vs 45.23. DROP non-football: 74.77 vs 82.45; football 59.56 vs 73.42.
limits: Gain is large on length generalisation, small on GSM8K. Hand-built prompts. Older models.
agent_relevance: Decomposition helps on harder, longer problems and does little or hurts on short ones; same conditional shape as MA94.

source: Press et al. (2022) Measuring and narrowing the compositionality gap in language models
finding: Compositionality gap: share of two-hop questions answered wrongly although both one-hop sub-questions are answered correctly. It stayed near 40 percent from small to large GPT-3 models. Self-ask makes the model write and answer follow-up questions, optionally using search.
numbers: Gap about 40 percent at every size (Figure 1). Davinci-002 accuracy on Bamboogle / 2Wiki / Musique: direct 17.6 / 25.4 / 5.6; chain of thought 46.4 / 29.8 / 12.6; self-ask 57.6 / 30.0 / 13.8; self-ask plus search 60.0 / 40.1 / 15.2. Later gaps: 42.9 percent ChatGPT, 23.0 percent GPT-4.
limits: Table 1 column order was inferred from the garbled extract. Bamboogle is 125 questions judged by the authors. Hand-chosen prompts.
agent_relevance: Writing and answering sub-questions beats direct answers on multi-hop; scale alone does not close the gap.

source: Khot et al. (2022) Decomposed prompting: a modular approach for solving complex tasks
finding: A decomposer prompt writes a program of sub-task calls; each sub-task has its own prompt, model or code. Tasks: kth letter concatenation, list reversal (recursive split), CommaQA-E, open-domain multi-hop QA.
numbers: Error analysis: remaining errors in letter concatenation and CommaQA are mostly sub-task errors, not decomposition errors. Letter concatenation stays close to 100 percent as list length grows while chain of thought degrades with length. Exact EM values are in figures I did not read.
limits: Figure values not extracted; claims follow the paper's text.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting so each part is a small checkable call and swapping a weak sub-step for code.

source: Synthesis of a04, a05 and a19 (no new source)
finding: Humans: decomposition helps when the true value is extreme and unknown (about 20-fold error cut) and hurts when it is familiar (458 percent error rise). LLMs: decomposition helps most on long or compositional tasks (SCAN 16.7 -> 99.7) and little on easy ones (GSM8K two-step slightly worse).
numbers: See a05 and a19.
limits: Different tasks, models and metrics; the parallel is by shape, not a pooled estimate.
agent_relevance: Trigger O3 on a hardness or magnitude-uncertainty signal (for example wide spread across samples), not by default. Fits guardrail G1.

source: Synthesis of a01, a08 and a13 (no new source)
finding: Decomposition needs uncorrelated part errors. A wrong anchor in a shared component multiplies through: US population misjudged by factor 1.97 in MA94; a bad fact in Kalyan Table 3 ends three orders of magnitude off.
numbers: +20 and +20 percent -> +44 percent; factor 1.97; three orders of magnitude.
limits: Inference from reported cases, not a direct LLM test.
agent_relevance: Insert known values from a tool for shared components and check parts against reference classes (links to subfield 04, outside view).

source: Gap statement (no new source)
finding: None of the opened sources tests decomposition against direct estimation for an LLM on real forecasting questions scored by Brier. Halawi uses sub-questions only for search. FermiEval and Kalyan cover Fermi estimation, not event forecasts.
numbers: No effect size available for LLM forecasting decomposition.
limits: Search budget ended before I could look for 2024-2026 decomposition-for-forecasting papers; absence here is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Run our own ablation: O3 on vs off on a forecasting set, scored by Brier.

source: MacGregor & Armstrong (1994) Judgmental decomposition: when does it work?
finding: The authors admit that the digit cut-off for extreme is arbitrary, that the unit of measure (miles vs inches) changes the digit count, and that problem selection may have affected the results.
numbers: Definition changed from more than 7 digits to 7 or more digits after the reanalysis.
limits: Single lab, volunteers recruited by newspaper ads at the University of Oregon.
agent_relevance: Use relative magnitude uncertainty (log-spread of samples) instead of digit count.
